title: Come and dine (John 21:1–14)
hookLine: a hundred and fifty-three fish, and breakfast on the shore

lines: A STRANGER ON THE SHORE AT DAWN.
cards: After everything in Jerusalem, the disciples go back to Galilee, and Peter says, in the King James Bible, "I go a fishing." Six others say, we'll come too.
Maybe that's what hands do after an upheaval: go back to what they know. They fish all night on the Sea of Tiberias and catch nothing. At dawn a man stands on the shore.
They don't recognize him. He calls out the way you'd call to a group of boys: children, have you any meat? Got anything to eat?

teach.b: Cast the net on the right side of the ship, he says, and ye shall find. They do, and suddenly they can't haul it in for the weight of fish.
The beloved disciple, who outran Peter to the tomb, understands first again: "It is the Lord."

teach.h: IT IS THE LORD, AND PETER JUMPS.
teach.b: Peter, being Peter, grabs his coat and jumps into the sea, and the others row in, dragging the net.
On land, "they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread." A fire of coals. There was one before, in the courtyard, where Peter warmed his hands and said, I am not.
Hold onto that for tomorrow. Then the number.

teach.h: A HUNDRED FIFTY-THREE, AND NO TEAR.
teach.b: Peter drags the net ashore, "full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken." Why count? Maybe someone simply did, the way fishermen tally a catch.
Ancient readers went further. Jerome said ancient naturalists counted a hundred fifty-three kinds of fish, so the net held every kind of person.
Augustine noticed that a hundred fifty-three is the sum of every number from one to seventeen. The text doesn't explain. Some see the unbroken net as a picture of a church big enough for everyone.
Then: "Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine." Breakfast. He's already cooked.
The risen Lord, on a beach, making breakfast for tired fishermen.

how: Many churches read this story in the Easter season, and some Christians remember it at shared meals and church breakfasts.

o: the fisherman who first said, it is the Lord
an early reader who added up one to seventeen
an early reader who saw all peoples in the catch

games.q: what's inside John 21:1–14 — tap the pairs.
p: great fishes, and the net held

s: the disciples recognize Jesus on the shore right away
they don't. the beloved disciple realizes it after the catch: "It is the Lord."
John counts this as the third time the risen Jesus showed himself to the disciples
John 21:14 says so: the third time, after he was risen from the dead.
the net tore under the weight of the fish
"for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken."

games.q: you're Peter in the boat. someone says, 'it is the Lord.' the shore is about two hundred cubits off. what do you do?
o: grab your coat and jump into the sea.
games.why: Peter girds his fisher's coat on and throws himself into the sea, leaving the others to bring in the net.

practice: Think of someone who's had a long night, literally or not, a roommate, a coworker on the early shift, a parent with a new baby, and picture making them something simple, toast, coffee, fruit on a plate, and handing it over without asking for anything back.
If you pray, give thanks for whoever has fed you; if not, remember the last time someone cooked for you.

wordCard.voice: Jerome. An early reader who said the catch of a hundred fifty-three fish stood for every kind of person the net could hold.

orig.note: Greek: come, have breakfast. ariston was the morning meal.

carryVoice: Your line: he's already cooked. Breakfast was waiting before they reached the shore. Day six hundred fifty-four, done.
